marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q001.takeaway: Severe cerebral ischemia strongly activates medullary vasomotor centers, making the CNS ischemic response the most powerful sympathetic activator.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q001.displayText:
Severe cerebral ischemia strongly activates medullary vasomotor centers, making the CNS ischemic response the most powerful sympathetic activator.

The most powerful activator of the sympathetic vasomotor system is CNS ischemic response.

CNS ischemic response:

When blood flow to the vasomotor center in lower brainstem (medulla) is severely decreased, the
local concentration of CO2 increases greatly and has a potent effect in stimulating the sympathetic
vasomotor nervous control areas in the brain’s medulla. Blood pressure may increase till 250
mmHg. The strong activation may cause some peripheral vessels to occlude.

It doesnt activate till arterial pressure drops to 60mmHg or less, hence it is principally a
emergency mechanism.

Note: Baroreceptors are the most common activators, but not the most powerful.
emphasis: Severe cerebral ischemia strongly activates medullary vasomotor centers, making the CNS ischemic response the most powerful sympathetic activator.

rationales.a: Postural responses help maintain pressure but are not the emergency CNS ischemic response described as most powerful.
rationales.b: Chemoreceptors can increase sympathetic activity, but the source distinguishes the CNS ischemic response as stronger.
rationales.d: Baroreceptors are frequent regulators of pressure, but the source explicitly distinguishes them from the most powerful activator.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q002.takeaway: Cerebral blood flow is relatively spared during exercise because cerebral vessels have poor vasoconstrictor innervation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q002.displayText:
Cerebral blood flow is relatively spared during exercise because cerebral vessels have poor vasoconstrictor innervation.

During exercise, the organ experiencing the smallest decrease in blood flow is brain.

489

both these circulatory areas have poor vasoconstrictor innervation .
emphasis: Cerebral blood flow is relatively spared during exercise because cerebral vessels have poor vasoconstrictor innervation.

rationales.b: Intestinal flow decreases as blood is redistributed during exercise, unlike the relatively spared cerebral circulation.
rationales.c: Renal flow decreases with sympathetic redistribution during exercise more than cerebral flow.
rationales.d: Non-exercising skeletal muscle is not spared to the same degree as cerebral and coronary circulations.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q005.takeaway: Pulmonary and systemic circulations are arranged in series, so their minute blood flows are approximately equal at steady state.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q005.displayText:
Pulmonary and systemic circulations are arranged in series, so their minute blood flows are approximately equal at steady state.

Blood flow per minute in the pulmonary circulation is equal to flow through the systemic
circulation so as to provide continuous blood supply to the body.

If the flow rate is slower in the pulmonary circulation than systemic, then the left ventricle would
soon empty completely. If the flow rate is faster in the pulmonary circulation then the left
ventricle would be soon overloaded.

Please note that because some blood flows into the bronchial arteries, the actual flow through the
pulmonary circulation is slightly lesser than the flow through the systemic circulation. However,
this question aims to state that the blood flow through both pulmonary and systemic circulation is
largely equal.

490
emphasis: Pulmonary and systemic circulations are arranged in series, so their minute blood flows are approximately equal at steady state.

rationales.a: A persistently lower pulmonary flow would drain the left ventricle because less blood would return from the lungs.
rationales.b: A persistently higher pulmonary flow would overload the left ventricle; steady series circuits carry approximately equal flow.
rationales.d: Pulmonary flow is not independent: it must match systemic flow in the series circulation, apart from minor bronchial contribution.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q007.takeaway: The umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood from placenta toward the fetus.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q007.displayText:
The umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood from placenta toward the fetus.

During fetal life, the vessel with maximum concentration of oxygen is umbilical vein.
emphasis: The umbilical vein carries the most oxygenated fetal blood from placenta toward the fetus.

rationales.a: The IVC receives mixed blood from multiple fetal streams and is less oxygenated than placental umbilical venous blood.
rationales.b: Fetal aortic blood is mixed after cardiac circulation and does not retain the highest oxygen concentration.
rationales.d: Umbilical arteries carry blood from fetus toward placenta for oxygenation; the return vessel is the umbilical vein.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q008.takeaway: Progressive hemorrhagic shock causes sluggish microvascular flow, tissue acidosis and small-vessel clotting.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q008.displayText:
Progressive hemorrhagic shock causes sluggish microvascular flow, tissue acidosis and small-vessel clotting.

Progressive hemorrhagic shock is characterized by the presence of blood clots in the small blood
vessels.

The initiating cause of this blockage is sluggish blood flow in the microvessels. Tissue metabolites
plus other deterioration products from the ischemic tissues causes minute clots in these vessels.
Thus the microvasculature gets blocked by the sludged blood.

In progressive hemorrhagic shock, there is increased lysosomal activity, decreased active
transport of sodium and tissue acidosis.
emphasis: Progressive hemorrhagic shock causes sluggish microvascular flow, tissue acidosis and small-vessel clotting.

rationales.b: The source describes increased, not decreased, lysosomal activity during progressive hemorrhagic shock.
rationales.c: Cellular sodium transport falls as ATP-dependent pump function deteriorates; it does not increase.
rationales.d: Ischemic tissue accumulates acidic metabolites, so the source describes acidosis rather than alkalosis.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q010.takeaway: Septic shock can have high cardiac output because systemic vasodilation lowers resistance while metabolic demand rises.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q010.displayText:
Septic shock can have high cardiac output because systemic vasodilation lowers resistance while metabolic demand rises.

Septic shock is characterized by high cardiac output.
High cardiac output in septic shock is caused by
+ arteriolar dilation in the infected tissues and

* high metabolic rate and vasodilation (resulting from bacterial toxin stimulating cellular
metabolism and from high body temperature).
emphasis: Septic shock can have high cardiac output because systemic vasodilation lowers resistance while metabolic demand rises.

rationales.a: Hemorrhagic shock reduces circulating volume and generally lowers venous return and cardiac output.
rationales.b: Cardiogenic shock is pump failure and therefore does not produce the high-output pattern described for septic shock.
rationales.d: Vasovagal shock involves vagal bradycardia and vasodilation, not the source’s high-output septic pattern.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q011.takeaway: Laplace’s relation links vessel radius to wall tension; a capillary’s very small radius limits circumferential tension at a given pressure.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q011.displayText:
Laplace’s relation links vessel radius to wall tension; a capillary’s very small radius limits circumferential tension at a given pressure.

The source applies Laplace’s law to explain why a capillary’s small radius limits wall tension at a given distending pressure. For a thin-walled cylindrical vessel, circumferential wall tension per unit length is proportional to pressure × radius (T = P × r); wall stress also depends on wall thickness.
emphasis: Laplace’s relation links vessel radius to wall tension; a capillary’s very small radius limits circumferential tension at a given pressure.

rationales.a: Poiseuille’s law relates flow to pressure gradient, viscosity, tube length and radius; it is not the wall-tension relation.
rationales.c: Frank–Starling describes how myocardial fiber stretch affects contraction, not capillary wall tension.
rationales.d: Fick’s law describes diffusion across a barrier, not the pressure-radius relation governing vessel wall tension.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q012.takeaway: Poiseuille’s law relates tube flow to pressure gradient, viscosity, length and the fourth power of radius.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q012.displayText:
Poiseuille’s law relates tube flow to pressure gradient, viscosity, length and the fourth power of radius.

The relationship between the flow in a long narrow tube, the viscosity of the fluid, and the radius of the tube is expressed mathematically by Poiseuille's law.

Poiseuille-Hagen formula:
F = (PA − PB) × (π/8) × (1/η) × (1/L) × r⁴

Where F = flow; PA − PB = pressure difference between two ends of the tube; η = viscosity; r = radius; L = length.
emphasis: Poiseuille’s law relates tube flow to pressure gradient, viscosity, length and the fourth power of radius.

rationales.a: Laplace’s law relates pressure, radius and wall tension; the question asks the flow relation for a tube.
rationales.c: Fick’s law concerns diffusion across a barrier, not bulk flow through a long narrow tube.
rationales.d: Frank–Starling relates cardiac filling/stretch to stroke output, not viscosity and tube radius.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q013.takeaway: Poiseuille flow varies with the fourth power of radius; the keyed comparison is 8-fold, while the source prose’s doubled-radius example would yield 16-fold flow.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q013.displayText:
Poiseuille flow varies with the fourth power of radius; the keyed comparison is 8-fold, while the source prose’s doubled-radius example would yield 16-fold flow.

The relationship between flow in a long narrow tube, viscosity, and radius is expressed mathematically by Poiseuille's law. Blood flow (F) inside the vessel depends on pressure difference, viscosity, radius and length. Radius is inversely proportional to resistance to the fourth power. Therefore, if the radius is doubled, resistance decreases by 2⁴ = 16; hence flow increases 16-fold for the same pressure difference.

Source consistency note: The keyed answer is 8-fold, but the following source sentence gives a doubled-radius example as 16-fold. Poiseuille’s fourth-power relation supports 16-fold for an actual 2:1 radius ratio; the omitted/embedded vessel figure is needed to establish the ratio that produces the keyed 8-fold answer. The key remains unchanged, and the figure-specific ratio is not reconstructed here.
emphasis: Poiseuille flow varies with the fourth power of radius; the keyed comparison is 8-fold, while the source prose’s doubled-radius example would yield 16-fold flow.

rationales.a: A fourfold flow ratio is not the source key; the stated vessel comparison is keyed as eightfold under the question’s figure conditions.
rationales.b: A 32-fold ratio is not the source key; Poiseuille flow changes with the fourth power of the radius ratio.
rationales.d: Sixteenfold flow is the result of doubling radius, as the explanation text says, but conflicts with the keyed 8-fold figure-specific answer.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q014.takeaway: The ebb phase conserves energy after injury; the later flow phase is hypermetabolic and activates acute-phase and innate immune responses.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q014.displayText:
The ebb phase conserves energy after injury; the later flow phase is hypermetabolic and activates acute-phase and innate immune responses.

The "flow" phase (not "ebb") leads to activation of the innate immune system and induction of the
hepatic acute-phase response.
Cuthbertson's ebb and flow response to trauma:

The "ebb" phase lasts for a brief duration and is associated with a decline in body temperature and
oxygen consumption, aimed at reducing post traumatic energy depletion.

The "flow" phase occurs after resuscitation from a state of shock, which leads to an increased
metabolic turnover, activation of the innate immune system and induction of the hepatic
acute-phase response. This hypercatabolic condition leads to a significantly increased oxygen
consumption and energy expenditure.

494
emphasis: The ebb phase conserves energy after injury; the later flow phase is hypermetabolic and activates acute-phase and innate immune responses.

rationales.a: A fall in temperature and oxygen consumption characterizes the ebb response, so this statement is true.
rationales.b: The source places the flow phase after resuscitation from shock, making this statement true.
rationales.c: The ebb phase’s reduced metabolism limits post-traumatic energy depletion; this statement is true.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q017.takeaway: Mayer waves are slow arterial-pressure oscillations generated by delayed reflex changes in neural blood-pressure control.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q017.displayText:
Mayer waves are slow arterial-pressure oscillations generated by delayed reflex changes in neural blood-pressure control.

Mayer waves are due to the variation of arterial pressure due to reflex changes in nervous control
of blood pressure.
The most important mechanisms are as follows:

I: Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflex:

High pressure excites the baroreceptors -->inhibits sympathetic nervous system and lowers the
pressure -->The decreased pressure, in turn, reduces the baroreceptor stimulation
-->elevating the pressure to a high value (the response is not instantaneous, it is delayed until a
few seconds later). This high pressure then initiates another cycle, and the oscillation continues.

II: Oscillation of the CNS Ischemic Response:

495, 

The cerebrospinal fluid pressure is raised to 160 mm Hg --> causes compression of cerebral
blood vessels --> cerebral ischemia--> CNS ischemic pressure response raises the arterial
pressure up to 200mm Hg -->the brain ischemia is relieved and the sympathetic nervous
system becomes inactive -->the arterial pressure falls rapidly back to a much lower value,
causing brain ischemia once again -->initiates another rise in pressure. This chain of events
repeats itself cyclically as long as the cerebrospinal fluid pressure remains elevated.
emphasis: Mayer waves are slow arterial-pressure oscillations generated by delayed reflex changes in neural blood-pressure control.

rationales.a: Beat-to-beat systolic variation is the pulse, not the slower Mayer-wave oscillation.
rationales.c: Respiration-linked pressure variation is a different oscillation from the delayed reflex cycle described for Mayer waves.
rationales.d: Postural changes can alter pressure but are not the reflex neural oscillation named Mayer waves.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q018.takeaway: Vasomotion is intermittent opening and closing of metarterioles and precapillary sphincters, modulated by local tissue oxygen.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH27_Q018.displayText:
Vasomotion is intermittent opening and closing of metarterioles and precapillary sphincters, modulated by local tissue oxygen.

Vasomotion is intermittent capillary perfusion caused by periodic contraction and relaxation of metarterioles and precapillary sphincters. Tissue oxygen concentration is the main local regulator described.
emphasis: Vasomotion is intermittent opening and closing of metarterioles and precapillary sphincters, modulated by local tissue oxygen.

rationales.a: IVC contraction is not the local rhythmic regulation of capillary perfusion called vasomotion.
rationales.c: Arterial pulsation can influence flow but does not define intermittent metarteriole and precapillary sphincter contraction.
rationales.d: The heartbeat ejecting into the aorta is cardiac systole, not local capillary vasomotion.
